examples.knowledge_point: Solving an Inequality When the Exponential is Compared to Zero or a Negative Number
examples.worked_solution:
Isolating the exponential term, we find

$$
\begin{aligned}4\cdot {3}^{8-x}+12 & >0 \\ 4\cdot {3}^{8-x} & >-12 \\ {3}^{8-x} & >-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Because a power of a positive number is always greater than $0,$ we must have

$$
3^{8-x} > 0
$$

for all values of $x.$

Therefore, the inequality $3^{8-x} > -3$ is satisfied for all real values of $x.$

feedback.worked_solution:
Isolating the exponential term, we find

$$
\begin{aligned}{(\frac{3}{4})}^{x+6}+1 & \ge 2 \\ {(\frac{3}{4})}^{x+6} & \ge 1.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, taking the natural logarithm of both sides and applying the laws of logarithms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡[{(\frac{3}{4})}^{x+6}] & \ge \operatorname{ln}⁡1 \\ (x+6)\operatorname{ln}⁡(\frac{3}{4}) & \ge 0 \\ (x+6)(\operatorname{ln}⁡3-\operatorname{ln}⁡4) & \ge 0 \\ (x+6)(\operatorname{ln}⁡3-2\operatorname{ln}⁡2) & \ge 0.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, note that $\operatorname{ln}⁡3-2\operatorname{ln}⁡2$ is a negative quantity, so when we divide both sides by it, we need to flip the inequality:

$$
\begin{aligned}(x+6) & \le \frac{0}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3-2\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\ x+6 & \le 0 \\ x & \le -6\end{aligned}
$$
